narrativeReportMd:
# DetectedIssue R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
`DetectedIssue` keeps the same canonical identity, but local R6 changes include hard R4-to-R6 instance breaks. The most important breaks are the required `status` value-set change, `patient` being replaced by generalized `subject`, and `severity` changing from a primitive code to CodeableConcept.

## Scope
The assessment used the local R4 and R6 core StructureDefinitions plus related local value sets and code systems named by DetectedIssue bindings. Base Resource/DomainResource/Element/BackboneElement changes are excluded and should be handled by their own artifact reports.

## Main migration themes
1. Several changes are wire-format breaks: `patient` becomes `subject`, and `severity` changes JSON shape.
2. Terminology and semantics changed: `status` no longer uses all ObservationStatus codes, and `code` is split from high-level `category`.
3. R6 is more expressive: it adds non-patient subjects, patient/caregiver authors, Timing for `identified[x]`, and several optional context/management fields that do not round-trip to base R4.

## Highest-impact findings
High-impact findings are `DetectedIssue.status` required-binding narrowing, `DetectedIssue.patient` to `DetectedIssue.subject`, `DetectedIssue.severity` code-to-CodeableConcept, and the semantic split of `code` versus `category`.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is especially needed for status-code mapping, R4 `code` values that may now belong in R6 `category`, R6 non-Patient subjects, R6 free-form CodeableConcept severity values, `identifiedTiming`, and R6-only management/evidence fields.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Some changes are probably justified by clearer modeling and broader workflows, but several could have been softened with deprecated transitional codes, cross-version ConceptMaps, or parallel richer elements.

## Follow-up analysis
Terminology expansion for v3 ActCode-backed value sets and an official spec clarification for `processing-error` in DetectedIssueStatus would improve confidence.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `DetectedIssue` has material local breaking changes despite stable artifact identity. Top concerns: `status` required-value-set change, `patient` to `subject`, `severity` primitive-to-CodeableConcept, and the `code`/`category` semantic split. Main uncertainty is terminology detail, especially v3 ActCode expansions and the R6 `processing-error` status inconsistency.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should be field-aware rather than purely syntactic. Patient references can usually be renamed to subject, severity codes must be wrapped as CodeableConcepts, and status values require clinical policy mapping. Code/category migration needs terminology and implementation review because validation may not catch semantic drift. Downgrade from R6 to R4 is lossy for non-Patient subjects, new author targets, `identifiedTiming`, and R6-only context/management fields.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural changes because both assigned StructureDefinitions were present and directly compared. Confidence is medium for some terminology and semantic conclusions because no official diff, full terminology expansions, or narrative ballot notes were supplied. The computable R6 DetectedIssueStatus value set and R6 status text disagree about `processing-error`, so that part needs specification review.

findings.title: DetectedIssue.status required binding changed from ObservationStatus to DetectedIssueStatus and removes several R4 status codes

oldState.summary: Required primitive code bound to ObservationStatus 4.0.1.

binding.description: Indicates the status of the identified issue.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R4 value set includes the complete R4 ObservationStatus code system. Local code-system evidence shows `registered`, `preliminary`, `final`, `amended`, `corrected`, `cancelled`, `entered-in-error`, and `unknown`.

semanticText.definition: Indicates the status of the detected issue.
semanticText.comment: R4 modifier rationale mentions cancelled and entered-in-error.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, `DetectedIssue.status` reused the Observation status lifecycle. Because the binding is `required`, any code in the R4 ObservationStatus value set was valid for this element.

newState.summary: Required primitive code bound to a DetectedIssue-specific status value set.

binding.description: Indicates the status of the identified issue.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R6 value set compose includes observation-status codes `preliminary`, `final`, `entered-in-error`, and `unknown`, plus detectedissue-status `mitigated`. The R6 StructureDefinition short/comment also mention `processing-error`, and the R6 detectedissue-status CodeSystem defines it, but the R6 value set compose examined locally does not include `processing-error`; this is treated as a ballot-build ambiguity rather than an allowed value.

semanticText.short: preliminary | final | entered-in-error | unknown | mitigated | processing-error
semanticText.definition: The current state of the detected issue.

newState.narrativeMd: In R6, `DetectedIssue.status` has its own required Detected Issue Status value set. The computable value set removes several R4 ObservationStatus codes and adds `mitigated`; the element text also discusses `processing-error`, but that code is not present in the R6 value set compose supplied in the package.

facts.note: These R4 ObservationStatus codes are not in the R6 DetectedIssueStatus value set compose.
The R6 DetectedIssueStatus value set compose includes `mitigated` from http://hl7.org/fhir/detectedissue-status.

facts.newValue: processing-error appears in the R6 StructureDefinition text and CodeSystem but not in the R6 ValueSet compose

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `DetectedIssue.status` has the same element id, path, type, cardinality, modifier flag, and summary flag in both releases; the material delta is the required terminology domain and status semantics.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation break for R4 instances using removed required-binding codes such as `registered`, `amended`, `corrected`, or `cancelled`. It is also a generated-enum and switch-logic risk because R4 implementations may have enum members that are no longer valid for DetectedIssue, while R6 introduces at least `mitigated`. R6-to-R4 mapping is lossy for `mitigated` because R4 DetectedIssue.status cannot carry it as a valid ObservationStatus code.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Status controls whether a DetectedIssue is current, withdrawn, or mitigated. Mis-mapping `cancelled`, `entered-in-error`, or `mitigated` can change whether alerts are displayed or suppressed.

justification.inferredGoal: Move DetectedIssue away from the Observation lifecycle and express statuses that are specific to detected-issue processing and mitigation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain removed R4 ObservationStatus codes as deprecated legacy codes in the R6 status value set while adding DetectedIssue-specific codes such as mitigated.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: A DetectedIssue-specific status lifecycle is a reasonable R6 goal, especially because status is mandatory and a modifier. The less-breaking base option is real, but it is only partial: allowing legacy ObservationStatus values such as `registered`, `amended`, or `cancelled` to remain valid would preserve old data while weakening the semantic cleanup and potentially affecting alert display or suppression logic. The local R6 package also has a `processing-error` text/value-set inconsistency, so the exact terminology still merits review.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best base-design alternative would include the removed R4 status codes in the R6 required value set as deprecated or legacy concepts while adding `mitigated` and any intended DetectedIssue-specific processing state. A ConceptMap alone would be migration guidance, not a backward-compatible base design. Keeping the old codes valid is only a partial alternative because consumers would still need to interpret observation-oriented lifecycle values safely in a DetectedIssue-specific modifier element.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves legacy instances but keeps observation-lifecycle concepts on a modifier status and can blur current, mitigated, and error semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 status has a required binding to http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/observation-status|4.0.1.
R4 ObservationStatus defines registered, preliminary, final, amended, corrected, cancelled, entered-in-error, and unknown.
R6 status has a required binding to http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/detectedissue-status|6.0.0-ballot4.
R6 DetectedIssueStatus includes preliminary, final, entered-in-error, unknown, and mitigated in the computable compose.
R6 CodeSystem defines processing-error, but the R6 DetectedIssueStatus ValueSet compose inspected locally does not include that code.

examples.examplesMd: The examples isolate the status field. A production migration must decide whether each removed R4 status can be mapped to `preliminary`, `final`, `entered-in-error`, `unknown`, `mitigated`, or a retained extension.

findings.narrativeMd: `DetectedIssue.status` is still mandatory and still a modifier, but the allowed required-binding codes changed materially. Old R4 data that used ObservationStatus lifecycle values such as `cancelled`, `amended`, `corrected`, or `registered` can fail R6 validation. Conversely, R6 can express `mitigated`, which has no valid primitive status equivalent in R4 DetectedIssue.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation fails when an instance carries a removed required-binding status code. Runtime failures are likely in generated enum models, status transition logic, alert-suppression code, and switch statements. R6-to-R4 conversion of `mitigated` is not lossless; `processing-error` needs human review because the R6 ElementDefinition text and CodeSystem mention it but the supplied ValueSet compose does not include it.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory all R4 DetectedIssue.status values before migration. Map straightforward continuing records to `preliminary`, `final`, `entered-in-error`, or `unknown` only when clinically correct. Treat `cancelled`, `amended`, `corrected`, and `registered` as policy decisions rather than automatic string substitutions. Preserve the original R4 status in an extension or Provenance/audit trail when the mapping is not exact. Test validation against the R6 DetectedIssueStatus value set rather than the element short text alone.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The DetectedIssue-specific lifecycle is reasonable, but the break could have been softened by including legacy ObservationStatus codes as deprecated transitional codes or by publishing an explicit cross-version ConceptMap. The tradeoff would be a less precise R6 status value set.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confirm whether `processing-error` is intended to be in the R6 DetectedIssueStatus value set. The local ballot package is internally inconsistent on that code.

findings.title: DetectedIssue.patient was replaced by DetectedIssue.subject and subject target types were broadened

semanticText.definition: Indicates the patient whose record the detected issue is associated with.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 modeled the associated record owner as `DetectedIssue.patient`, constrained to Reference(Patient).

newState.summary: Optional subject reference with many possible target resource types.

semanticText.definition: Indicates the subject whose record the detected issue is associated with.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 replaces the patient-specific element with `DetectedIssue.subject` and allows Patient, Group, Device, Location, Organization, Procedure, Practitioner, Medication, Substance, BiologicallyDerivedProduct, or NutritionProduct references.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The elements have the same role in the resource, same cardinality, same summary flag, and parallel definitions, but the path changed from patient-specific to generalized subject and the target domain was widened.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An R4 JSON instance containing `patient` will contain an unknown element in R6 and will not populate the new `subject` field. Generated R4 client code commonly exposes a `patient` property, while R6 code exposes `subject`; code, FHIRPath, search logic, and transforms must change. R6 instances whose subject is not a Patient cannot be represented in the R4 `patient` slot without an extension or lossy omission.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The associated subject determines whose record, access controls, and alert context the issue belongs to. Dropping or misidentifying it can route a clinical warning to the wrong context.

justification.inferredGoal: Align DetectedIssue with the broader Event subject pattern and allow non-patient detected issues.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 `patient` path, broaden its target profiles to the R6 subject set, and update the definition and aliases to associated subject semantics.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Generalizing the associated entity beyond Patient is a reasonable R6 goal, but the hard wire-format rename was not necessary to accomplish it. Because FHIR JSON has no aliasing mechanism, replacing `patient` with `subject` invalidates common R4 payloads and generated APIs. Retaining the old path with broader targets would have met the main functional goal with a moderate naming tradeoff, so the break looks probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base R6 design would leave `DetectedIssue.patient` as the canonical element, broaden its allowed targets to Patient plus the non-patient subject resources, and clarify that the historical name now means the associated subject or record context. Adding a new parallel `subject` while retaining `patient` would be only a partial transition because two same-resource fields could conflict; simply living with the old path avoids that duplication.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances without duplicate fields; the cost is a misleading legacy element name and weaker consistency with subject-named Event resources.

evidence.detail: R4 defines DetectedIssue.patient as 0..1 Reference(Patient).
R6 defines DetectedIssue.subject as 0..1 Reference with Patient plus ten additional target profiles.
No R6 DetectedIssue.patient element exists in the local R6 StructureDefinition.

examples.examplesMd: Patient references can usually be renamed mechanically from `patient` to `subject`. R6 non-Patient subjects require a policy for R4 representation, typically an extension or omission with documented loss.

findings.narrativeMd: The patient element is effectively renamed and generalized. This is a hard wire-format break for R4 instances and a source-code break for generated models and FHIRPath expressions. It also changes the resource from patient-only context to a much broader subject domain.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `patient` are old-valid/new-invalid because `patient` is no longer a valid R6 element. R6 instances with `subject.reference` to Patient can be converted back to R4 `patient`; R6 subjects such as Medication, Device, Procedure, or Group cannot be represented in R4 without an extension or loss of subject context.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `patient` to `subject` for Patient references during R4-to-R6 migration. Update generated model accessors, search/indexing code, FHIRPath expressions, authorization rules, and displays that assumed `DetectedIssue.patient`. For R6-to-R4, only map Patient subjects to `patient`; preserve non-Patient subjects in an extension and flag the record for manual review if downstream behavior depends on subject type.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The broadened subject pattern is useful and aligns with other event resources, but the breaking rename could have been eased by retaining a deprecated patient element or by publishing a cross-version extension. That alternative would trade short-term compatibility for model duplication.

findings.title: DetectedIssue.severity changed from required-bound primitive code to preferred-bound CodeableConcept

oldState.summary: Optional primitive code with required binding to high | moderate | low.

binding.description: Indicates the potential degree of impact of the identified issue on the patient.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local R4 detectedissue-severity CodeSystem contains `high`, `moderate`, and `low`.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 represents severity as a primitive code string, constrained to the DetectedIssueSeverity value set.

newState.summary: Optional CodeableConcept with preferred binding to the same severity scale.

binding.description: Indicates the potential degree of impact of the identified issue on the patient.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local R6 detectedissue-severity CodeSystem still contains `high`, `moderate`, and `low`, but the binding is preferred and CodeableConcept permits other codings or text.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 changes the wire shape to a CodeableConcept and weakens the binding strength from required to preferred.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The path, cardinality, summary flag, and semantic purpose are the same; only the datatype and binding strength changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: FHIR JSON represents a primitive `code` as a string but represents a CodeableConcept as an object. Therefore an R4 instance with `"severity":"high"` is structurally invalid as R6. Generated models also change from a scalar/enum-like primitive to a complex coding object. R6-to-R4 conversion is only straightforward when a CodeableConcept contains one of the legacy high/moderate/low codings.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Severity often drives alert display priority and escalation. Lossy or incorrect conversion can alter triage behavior.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow richer severity coding, multiple coding systems, and text while retaining the old severity scale as preferred terminology.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain deprecated primitive `severity` and add a separate optional CodeableConcept severity element for richer codings.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Richer severity coding is a credible R6 goal, and a CodeableConcept can carry multiple coding systems, display text, and translations that the R4 primitive cannot. A less-breaking sibling-field design exists, but it would leave two ways to express severity, which is often used for alert priority and triage. Those conflict and implementation costs make the compatibility alternative only partial and the direct redesign probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The compatible base option would keep `DetectedIssue.severity` as the R4 primitive code, likely deprecated, and add a new element such as `severityConcept` for CodeableConcept content. A choice-type redesign would not preserve the old JSON member because it would introduce suffixed properties. The sibling approach preserves R4 instances but requires rules when both primitive and CodeableConcept severities are present or disagree.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old string/enum data but creates duplicate severity representations, precedence rules, and safety-sensitive conflict handling.

evidence.detail: R4 severity type is primitive code.
R4 severity has a required binding to detectedissue-severity|4.0.1.
R6 severity type is CodeableConcept.
R6 severity binding strength is preferred.
R4 and R6 local code systems both define high, moderate, and low.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example shows the usual scalar-to-CodeableConcept wrapping for legacy high/moderate/low values.

findings.narrativeMd: `DetectedIssue.severity` keeps the same name but changes datatype. That can be more surprising than a renamed element because serializers may still emit a `severity` member, but with the old primitive string shape that R6 no longer accepts.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with a populated severity primitive are old-valid/new-invalid. Empty severity is unaffected. R6 CodeableConcept values can only be losslessly converted to R4 when they contain a clear high/moderate/low coding from the legacy system; text-only, multi-coding, or local-scale severity values need manual policy.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Wrap R4 severity codes into a CodeableConcept using system `http://hl7.org/fhir/detectedissue-severity`. Update generated classes, JSON serializers, validation tests, and UI code that treated severity as a scalar enum. For R6-to-R4, choose a deterministic preferred coding when available and preserve richer CodeableConcept content in an extension or audit field when no legacy code is available.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The richer datatype likely reflects a valid terminology need, but the same goal could have been achieved by adding a parallel CodeableConcept field. The chosen direct replacement simplifies R6 but breaks old wire format and generated APIs.

findings.title: DetectedIssue.code no longer carries the high-level category; R6 adds category for categorization and changes the code binding

oldState.summary: Optional CodeableConcept described as the general issue type/category.

binding.description: Codes identifying the general type of detected issue.

semanticText.short: Issue Category, e.g. drug-drug, duplicate therapy, etc.
semanticText.definition: Identifies the general type of issue identified.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 used `DetectedIssue.code` as the issue category/general type, with a preferred binding to `detectedissue-category`.

newState.summary: Optional CodeableConcept for the specific issue type; high-level categorization moved to category 0..*.

binding.description: Codes identifying the type of detected issue.

semanticText.short: Specific type of detected issue, e.g. drug-drug, duplicate therapy, etc
semanticText.definition: A code that identifies the specific type of issue detected.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 keeps `code` but changes it to the specific issue code and adds `DetectedIssue.category` 0..* for high-level categorization. R6 category is preferred-bound to a short explicit set of v3 ActCode concepts such as FOOD, DRUG, ALGY, and DUPTHPY.

facts.oldValue: Issue Category, e.g. drug-drug, duplicate therapy, etc.
facts.newValue: Specific type of detected issue, e.g. drug-drug, duplicate therapy, etc

facts.oldValue: R4 detectedissue-category used ActCode is-a filters
facts.newValue: R6 detectedissue-category has explicit concepts FOOD, DRUG, ALGY, DUPTHPY

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `DetectedIssue.code` has the same path and datatype, but the text and binding show that its role changed from general category to specific issue code while a new `category` element takes over categorization. Because bindings are preferred, validation alone will not catch all semantic mis-migrations.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not a direct base validation break because both old and new `code` are optional CodeableConcept with preferred bindings. The breaking mechanism is semantic: R4 systems that used `code` for filtering, access control, duplicate therapy grouping, or alert category display may continue to validate but place values in the wrong R6 semantic slot. R6 instances can also carry multiple categories in `category`, which R4 has no separate native element for.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Detected-issue category can control alert routing and visibility. Misclassifying a specific code as a high-level category, or dropping R6 categories on downgrade, can change clinical decision-support behavior.

justification.inferredGoal: Separate high-level categorization from the specific detected issue code.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep R4 `code` as the high-level category and add a new specific issue-code element, with any repeatable category transition explicitly governed.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Separating high-level category from specific issue code is a reasonable model improvement. The concern is that R6 reuses the familiar `code` path with changed semantics, so many R4 instances can still validate while being interpreted in the wrong slot. A less-breaking design could have made the new specific-code concept explicit, and the supplied evidence does not show why silent repurposing of `code` was necessary.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would preserve `DetectedIssue.code` for the R4 category/general-type meaning and add a new `specificCode` or equivalent element for the more detailed R6 issue code. This is only a partial alternative because R6 also adds repeatable `category`; supporting multiple categories while keeping the old single `code` path may require an overlapping category element and precedence rules. Even so, it would make migration intent clearer than changing the meaning of an existing path.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids silent semantic drift but leaves awkward naming and either limits category multiplicity or creates overlap with a new category field.

evidence.detail: R4 code is described as issue category/general type and preferred-bound to detectedissue-category.
R6 code is described as the specific type of issue and preferred-bound to detectedissue-code.
R6 adds category 0..* CodeableConcept for high-level categorization.
R6 detectedissue-category explicitly includes FOOD, DRUG, ALGY, and DUPTHPY.
R6 detectedissue-code uses ActCode is-a filters for administration, supplied item, clinical action, and supply detected issue codes.

examples.examplesMd: The migration shape is illustrative only. Actual mapping from old R4 `code` values to R6 `category` and/or R6 `code` requires terminology review and possibly site-specific rules.

findings.narrativeMd: The same element name `code` survives, but its role changes. That makes this a likely silent break: data can validate while downstream logic reads it with the wrong meaning. R6 introduces `category` as the high-level filter/governance element and reserves `code` for the specific detected issue type.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Because the bindings are preferred, many mismapped CodeableConcepts will still validate. The compatibility problem is behavioral and semantic rather than schema-only. R6-to-R4 is lossy when multiple categories are present or when R6 category and specific code need to remain distinct.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not blindly copy R4 `code` to R6 `code` without reviewing what the source system placed there. If the R4 value was used as a high-level category, populate R6 `category`; if it was truly a specific issue code, populate R6 `code`; if it served both purposes, consider populating both with documented mapping rules. Update search parameters, indexes, display grouping, access-control logic, and CDS rule predicates that used `DetectedIssue.code` as a category.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The split improves modeling precision, but retaining the name `code` for a changed semantic role is migration-hostile. An explicit transition element or ConceptMap could have reduced silent behavior drift.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confidence is lower than for structural findings because the v3 ActCode filter expansions were not locally expanded and real-world R4 use of `code` may vary by implementation.

findings.title: DetectedIssue.identified[x] gained Timing and changed from initial identification time to occurrence/ongoing timing

oldState.summary: Optional dateTime or Period for when the issue was initially identified.

semanticText.definition: The date or period when the detected issue was initially identified.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed `identifiedDateTime` or `identifiedPeriod` and described the value as when the detected issue was initially identified.

newState.summary: Optional dateTime, Period, or Timing for when the detected issue occurred or is occurring.

semanticText.definition: The date, period or timing when the detected issue did occur or is occurring.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `identifiedTiming` and reframes the element as occurrence or ongoing timing rather than only initial identification date/period.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The same choice element is present in both releases; R6 adds a choice type and changes explanatory text.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Existing R4 `identifiedDateTime` and `identifiedPeriod` values remain in the R6 type set, so this is not an old-valid/new-invalid break. The risk is that generated choice-type code and business logic must now handle `identifiedTiming`, and the semantic text no longer strictly means the initial detection timestamp. R6 Timing values cannot be represented in R4 without flattening or extensions.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Timing may affect whether a DetectedIssue is displayed as active or historical, but the element remains optional.

justification.inferredGoal: Support recurring or ongoing issue timing rather than only a timestamp or period.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `identified[x]` as the initial detection time and add a separate occurrence or occurrenceTiming element for ongoing or recurring timing.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding support for recurring or ongoing timing is reasonable, but changing the meaning of `identified[x]` from initial identification to occurrence timing creates avoidable semantic drift. Detection time and occurrence time are related but distinct facts, so a separate occurrence-oriented element would meet the R6 goal while preserving existing interpretation of R4 `identifiedDateTime` and `identifiedPeriod` data.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The less-breaking base design would retain `identified[x]` with its R4 definition and add a new optional occurrence choice, including Timing, for when the issue occurred or is occurring. This would not require duplicate representations of the same fact; it would model two temporal facts explicitly. The tradeoff is an additional element and the need for guidance when only one of detection time or occurrence timing is known.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 semantics with modest extra model surface; implementers must distinguish detection time from occurrence timing.

evidence.detail: R4 types are dateTime and Period.
R6 types are dateTime, Period, and Timing.
R4 definition says when the detected issue was initially identified.
R6 definition says when the detected issue did occur or is occurring.

examples.examplesMd: A Timing can sometimes be approximated as a Period for R4, but recurrence details are lost.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 widens the choice type and changes the meaning from initial identification to occurrence or ongoing timing. This is not a direct R4-to-R6 validation break, but it is a migration and interpretation risk for generated choice handlers and clinical logic.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 dateTime and Period instances remain representable in R6. R6 Timing instances are not native R4 DetectedIssue content. Code that enumerates known choice suffixes must add `identifiedTiming` and should not assume the field is only the initial identification moment.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Carry R4 `identifiedDateTime` and `identifiedPeriod` forward as-is unless local requirements distinguish initial detection time from occurrence time. Add tests for all three R6 choices. For R6-to-R4, preserve Timing in an extension or map only a bounds Period when loss is acceptable.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The additive type is backward-compatible for R4-to-R6 validation but not for reverse conversion. The semantic change could have been clearer with a new occurrence element and a retained identified element.

findings.title: DetectedIssue.author can now be Patient or RelatedPerson as well as practitioner/device actors

oldState.summary: Optional author reference to Practitioner, PractitionerRole, or Device.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 limits the author to clinical/professional or device actors.

newState.summary: Optional author reference also allowing Patient and RelatedPerson.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds Patient and RelatedPerson to the author target profile list.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element path and meaning are stable; the target domain is widened.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 author references remain valid in R6. R6 DetectedIssue instances authored by a Patient or RelatedPerson cannot be represented in the R4 author field. Generated type unions, authorization rules, and displays that assume an author is a practitioner/device actor must be updated.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The author can affect accountability and display, but the element is optional and not a modifier.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow patient- or caregiver-originated detected issue reports.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: R6 widens `author` targets while retaining all R4 author target types.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Allowing Patient and RelatedPerson authors supports patient- and caregiver-originated detected-issue workflows and does not invalidate R4 author references. The remaining compatibility costs are generated-code/runtime assumptions and downgrade handling for new R6 targets, not a less-breaking R6 base-design question for preserving R4 instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No backward-compatible base alternative is needed for R4-to-R6 preservation because Practitioner, PractitionerRole, and Device remain valid author targets. Using extensions or a separate reporter field for Patient or RelatedPerson would be a downgrade or R4-backport mitigation, not evidence of a better backward-compatible R6 base design.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6-to-R4 conversion and closed-union client assumptions need policy, but that is not an R4-to-R6 base preservation problem.

evidence.detail: R4 author targets Practitioner, PractitionerRole, and Device.
R6 author also targets Patient and RelatedPerson.

examples.examplesMd: An R6 Patient or RelatedPerson author should not be coerced into an R4 Practitioner/Device reference.

findings.narrativeMd: `DetectedIssue.author` is widened, not narrowed. R4 data migrates forward, but systems that downgrade R6 data or enforce old actor assumptions must account for Patient and RelatedPerson authors.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: There is no old-valid/new-invalid break for R4 target profiles. The compatibility risk is R6-to-R4 and runtime: old generated validators or business rules may reject or mishandle Patient/RelatedPerson authors.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update reference-target validation and actor display logic. For R6-to-R4, preserve Patient/RelatedPerson authors in an extension or Provenance record rather than dropping accountability silently.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This is a reasonable additive target expansion. A backward-compatible R4 path would require extensions, which are less interoperable than a native R6 target list.

findings.title: DetectedIssue.detail changed from string to markdown

semanticText.definition: A textual explanation of the detected issue.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 stores `detail` as a plain string.

semanticText.definition: A textual explanation of the detected issue.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 stores `detail` as markdown, which is still serialized as a JSON string but has different generated primitive types and rendering expectations.

facts.note: FHIR primitive JSON shape remains a scalar string, but generated primitive classes and rendering semantics differ.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Same path, cardinality, and definition; datatype changed from string to markdown.

impact.impactRationaleMd: A valid R4 plain string should still serialize as a JSON string acceptable for an R6 markdown primitive, so this is not a hard wire-format break. The main risk is generated code, schema-specific serializers, UI rendering, sanitization, and systems that treat markdown formatting as executable presentation rather than literal text.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect rendering or sanitization could alter display, but the field is explanatory text and not a modifier.

justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `detail` typed as `string` and state in the definition or rendering guidance that markdown syntax may be used.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Formatted issue detail text is a reasonable goal, and the wire representation remains a JSON string. However, changing the primitive type still creates type-aware code generation, schema, rendering, and sanitization churn. The same practical formatting goal could mostly be met by retaining `string` with clearer markdown guidance, so the type-level break is not clearly justified by the supplied evidence.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible base design would leave `DetectedIssue.detail` as `string` and update the definition, comment, or implementation guidance to say that markdown content may appear and should be rendered safely. This preserves R4 instances and generated string properties. The tradeoff is that generic R6 tooling would not infer markdown behavior solely from the primitive type.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves generated-type compatibility while losing the computable primitive-type signal for markdown rendering and sanitization.

evidence.detail: R4 detail type is string.
R6 detail type is markdown.

examples.examplesMd: No old-valid/new-invalid JSON fragment is provided because both FHIR primitive types are serialized as JSON strings. The risk is generated primitive type and rendering behavior.

findings.narrativeMd: `DetectedIssue.detail` is a code-generation and display risk rather than a typical instance-validation break. R6 consumers may render Markdown and apply markdown-specific sanitization, while R4 consumers likely treated the same content as plain text.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Plain R4 string content should remain structurally representable in R6. R6 markdown content can be copied into R4 string without losing characters, but R4 consumers will not know it is intended as markdown. Generated classes may change from StringType/string to MarkdownType/markdown wrappers.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update generated model mappings and UI rendering. Treat migrated R4 detail text as literal markdown input and ensure HTML output is sanitized. For R6-to-R4, preserve the markdown source string and document that R4 consumers may display formatting markers literally.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This change is probably acceptable because it preserves the primitive JSON shape. The less-breaking alternative of keeping `string` would not express the new formatting semantics to tooling.

findings.title: R6 adds optional context, evidence, medication-class, management, and mitigation-note elements with no native R4 representation

oldState.summary: R4 has no native elements for encounter, qualityOfEvidence, expectedOnsetType, medicationClass, managementCode, or mitigation.note.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 DetectedIssue lacks these optional R6 context and management fields. Some information may have been carried in extensions or free text, but there is no standard R4 slot.

newState.summary: R6 adds six optional elements for encounter context, evidence quality, expected onset, medication class, management code, and mitigation notes.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `encounter` 0..1 Reference(Encounter), `qualityOfEvidence` 0..1 CodeableConcept, `expectedOnsetType` 0..1 CodeableConcept, `medicationClass` 0..* CodeableConcept, `managementCode` 0..1 CodeableConcept, and `mitigation.note` 0..* Annotation.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: These element ids are present in the R6 DetectedIssue snapshot and absent from the R4 DetectedIssue snapshot. They are optional, so they are additive for R4-to-R6 validation but not for downgrade or round-trip.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Optional additions do not invalidate R4 instances in R6. They do create native R6 content that cannot be represented in R4 DetectedIssue without extensions or lossy conversion. The highest risk fields are `managementCode` and `mitigation.note`, which may explain what action should be taken or why mitigation is acceptable.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Dropping management guidance, mitigation notes, expected onset, or evidence quality can remove context that clinicians or CDS systems use to judge alert urgency and reliability.

justification.inferredGoal: Add richer DetectedIssue context and management details to the base resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the added R6 context, evidence-quality, medication-class, management, and mitigation-note elements are optional and do not invalidate R4 instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding optional native fields for encounter context, evidence quality, expected onset, medication class, management code, and mitigation notes improves R6 expressivity without creating an old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 break. Native elements are a reasonable base design despite round-trip loss when converting new R6 content back to R4.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking R6 base design is needed to preserve R4 instances because these fields are additive and optional. Standardized R4 extensions could help cross-version conversion, but extensions are a backport or downgrade mitigation rather than a backward-compatible alternative to native optional R6 elements.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Downgrading to unprofiled R4 may need extensions or lose data, but that is an R6-to-R4 conversion issue rather than a less-breaking R6 base alternative.

evidence.detail: R6 adds encounter 0..1 Reference(Encounter), summary true.
R6 adds qualityOfEvidence 0..1 CodeableConcept.
R6 adds expectedOnsetType 0..1 CodeableConcept.
R6 adds medicationClass 0..* CodeableConcept.
R6 adds managementCode 0..1 CodeableConcept.
R6 adds mitigation.note 0..* Annotation.
No matching R4 DetectedIssue elements exist for these paths.

examples.examplesMd: The example shows R6 content that has no native R4 DetectedIssue element. An extension-based profile can preserve it, but an unprofiled R4 instance cannot.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds several optional fields that make DetectedIssue more expressive. These are not R4-to-R6 breaking, but they are significant for round-trip and downgrade workflows because dropping them can remove encounter context, evidence quality, expected clinical onset, medication class, management priority, or explanatory mitigation notes.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances remain valid with respect to these additions because all are optional. R6 instances using any of these fields are not cleanly representable in base R4. Strict R4 validators will reject the unknown elements unless they are transformed into extensions.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6, populate these fields only when source extensions or local data support them. For R6-to-R4, define cross-version extensions for each field that must survive downgrade, and add tests that verify no management or mitigation rationale is silently lost. If no extension strategy exists, flag affected records as lossy conversions.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because these are optional additions, the forward compatibility cost is low. The main backward-compatible alternative is publishing official cross-version extensions and ConceptMaps for the new terminology-backed fields.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, derivation, baseDefinition, and abstract flag are stable. Metadata maturity/status changes are noted as non-breaking.
No matched local element had a minimum increase or maximum decrease. `mitigation.action` remains 1..1; added R6 elements are optional.
No DetectedIssue-specific invariant was added, removed, or tightened. Generic `ele-1`, `dom-*`, and extension constraints are inherited/base-artifact scope.
`DetectedIssue.status` remains a modifier and no local non-inherited element gained or lost modifier status. Inherited modifierExtension behavior is out of scope.

Summary flags on matched local elements are stable. R6 adds optional summary elements `category` and `encounter`; those additive changes are covered in findings, not as flag changes on existing elements.
No local slicing or slice discriminator changes were present in the DetectedIssue snapshots.
No local fixed, pattern, or defaultValue constraints were found on DetectedIssue elements.
No local maxLength, regex, minValue, or maxValue changes were found for DetectedIssue.
Reference target changes for `subject` and `author` are covered as findings. `implicated`, `evidence.detail`, and `mitigation.author` target profiles are materially unchanged.

Material binding changes for `status`, `severity`, and `code`/`category` are findings. `evidence.code` and `mitigation.action` retained their binding strengths and canonical value-set identities at this level of analysis.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Governance and conformance programs may treat the R6 definition as more stable, but this should not be counted as an inherited or local instance-breaking change.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Root description adds gaps in care as an example

nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Implementers may see DetectedIssue used for gaps-in-care alerts in R6, but the change is illustrative rather than a direct validation break.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Identifier narrative clarifies business-identifier semantics
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The element path, cardinality, datatype, and summary flag are unchanged. The R6 text clarifies that identifiers are business identifiers and may remain constant across updates.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Systems should not confuse `identifier` with `Resource.id`, but no data transform is required solely because of this clarification.
